meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Beware the man of one book'?
meta.ogDescription: Not in Aquinas's works. A 1649 anecdote by Jeremy Taylor has him advise 'reading of one book'; the 'beware' warning is a later proverb.

answer.label: Not Thomas Aquinas — a later proverb
answer.authorDates: Tied to Aquinas through an anecdote in Jeremy Taylor’s The Great Exemplar (1649)
answer.sourceLine: The line does not appear in anything Aquinas wrote, and Wikiquote ↗ lists it as disputed. What can be documented is a second-hand story in Bishop Jeremy Taylor’s The Great Exemplar (1649). In it, Aquinas is asked how a man might best become learned and answers “By reading of one book.” That is advice to focus, not a warning. The “beware” wording is a later proverb built on that story.

source.heading: The anecdote behind the attribution

docMeta.dd: The Great Exemplar of Sanctity and Holy Life
Part II, Section XII, Discourse XII (“Of prayer”), §16
Whole Works, vol. II, ed. Reginald Heber, rev. Charles Page Eden (London, 1847)

source.excerpt: …so is the spirit of man busied in variety, and divided in itself: it abates its fervour, cools into indifferency, and becomes trifling by its dispersion and inadvertency. Aquinas was once asked, with what compendium a man might best become learned? he answered, By reading of one book: meaning, that an understanding entertained with several objects is intent upon neither, and profits not.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ lists Hominem unius libri timeo (“I fear the man of a single book”) under Disputed on its Aquinas page. Its only citation is Leonard Sweet’s 2012 book, and it gives “Beware the man of one book” as a variant.
Jeremy Taylor’s The Great Exemplar (1649) tells the story that Aquinas, asked how to become learned, answered “By reading of one book,” meaning a divided mind “profits not.” (1847 edition ↗)

Bartlett’s Familiar Quotations (ninth edition) lists “Beware of a man of one book” as a proverbial phrase on p. 853. It explains it with Robert Southey’s retelling of Taylor’s anecdote from The Doctor. (Project Gutenberg ↗)

Wikipedia ↗ notes that the phrase first praised mastery of one discipline, and John Wesley used it of himself and the Bible. Today it usually means the opposite: someone narrow, who has read only one book.
source.excerptNote: This is Taylor’s anecdote as printed in the 1847 edition of his works. The same passage appears in the 1649 printing. Taylor gives no source for the story, and in this passage Aquinas recommends one book; nobody is told to beware of anyone. The main text gives his answer only in English, not as the Latin timeo (“I fear”) phrase.

author.heading: About Thomas Aquinas
author.metaLine: c. 1225 – 1274 · Italian Dominican friar, theologian & philosopher
author.bio: Thomas Aquinas was an Italian Dominican friar and priest, and the leading theologian of medieval Scholasticism. He is best known for the Summa Theologiae. People have long credited him with the Latin Hominem unius libri timeo (“I fear the man of a single book”) and its English form “Beware the man of one book,” but neither has been found in his writings.

misattribution.heading: How a piece of advice became a warning
misattribution.intro: “Beware the man of one book” is usually credited to Thomas Aquinas, often with the Latin Hominem unius libri timeo. The paper trail does not support either.

items.why: No passage in Aquinas’s writings has been cited for it. Wikiquote ↗ files it under Disputed, and the Catholic writer Taylor Marshall says ↗ it is not in Aquinas’s works as far as he has read.
Taylor reports, with no source, that Aquinas answered “By reading of one book” when asked how to become learned. In this passage the one-book reader is the ideal, not someone to fear. (text ↗)

Bartlett’s ninth edition prints “Beware of a man of one book” as a proverbial heading and explains it with Southey’s retelling of Taylor. Southey says the homo unius libri is “proverbially formidable.” (Gutenberg ↗)

misattribution.truthLine: Aquinas is not known to have written “Beware the man of one book.” What can be documented is Jeremy Taylor’s unsourced 1649 story that Aquinas recommended “reading of one book,” and a later proverb that turned that advice into a warning. See Homo unius libri ↗.

context.heading: Why the meaning flipped
lead: In Taylor’s story, the “one book” is a mark of focus: an understanding “entertained with several objects is intent upon neither, and profits not.” Southey later called the homo unius libri “proverbially formidable,” meaning a debater who has mastered one text and is hard to beat on it.
The modern quotation runs the other way. It warns against the narrow reader who has read only one book. Wikipedia ↗ notes that this is now the usual sense, which reverses the earlier one.
detailsBody: Methodism’s founder John Wesley took up the phrase in the older, approving sense, with the one book being the Bible. In a letter to John Newton of 14 May 1765 he wrote, “in 1730 I began to be homo unius libri, to study (comparatively) no book but the Bible.” (as quoted on Wikipedia ↗)
